Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
make sure to stay close to exit
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette:
Carlos, a sixty-five-year-old special education teacher and divorced father of two, had served as a medic in the jungles of Central America decades ago. The event that shattered him occurred during a night patrol when his unit was ambushed near a muddy riverbank. A grenade blast sent him spinning; he landed hard, his head ringing, and as he tried to drag a wounded soldier to cover, he tasted something metallic and foul—a mix of blood, mud, and the bitter chemical residue of the explosion. He could still feel the dizziness that followed, the world tilting as he struggled to keep his hands steady on the tourniquet. He had not spoken of it in over thirty years, not even to his ex-wife, until a recent classroom incident forced the memories back.

Six months ago, during a fire drill at the middle school where he taught, a student accidentally set off a loud, unexpected alarm directly beside Carlos’s ear. The sound—a sharp, piercing blast—sent him reeling. His head swam with the old dizziness, and for a moment he tasted that same metallic grit on his tongue. He had to brace himself against the wall, his heart hammering, as he scanned the hallway for exits he already knew were there. After that day, the world felt different. The dizziness returned unpredictably, sometimes when he stood up too fast from his desk, other times during the gust of a passing truck. The taste would surface without warning, sour and metallic, often in the middle of a lesson, making him gag silently.

Carlos began to avoid anything that might stir strong emotions. He stopped joining colleagues for lunch, fearing a heated discussion about school politics could trigger the spinning sensation. He started sitting at the back of the staff room, near the door, and found himself mapping escape routes every time he entered a new room—the gymnasium, the principal’s office, even the church he attended on Sundays. The hypervigilance became a constant companion. Every unexpected sound—a door slamming, a chair scraping—made him flinch and freeze, his eyes darting to the nearest exit. He was certain that if he let his guard down, the dizziness would overwhelm him, and he would collapse in front of his students. This fear, in turn, made his threat monitoring worse: the more he planned his escape, the more he noticed potential threats, and the more he noticed, the more likely he was to feel the dizzying rush and the phantom taste.

The cycle tightened over the weeks. In the classroom, he could no longer talk about the event with other veterans at the local VFW, because even mentioning the ambush brought on the symptoms. He began to check his surroundings constantly, even in his own apartment, scanning for signs of danger—an open window, a shadow moving. His escape route planning became a ritual: before sitting down anywhere, he would mentally trace three paths to the nearest door. The loud noises at school became unbearable; he flinched at the bell, at the slam of a locker, at a child’s sudden shout. Each startle rekindled the dizziness and the taste, which then drove him to scan harder, to stay closer to the exit, to avoid any emotional engagement with his students or colleagues.

His work suffered. He stopped leading the after-school tutoring group because the room had only one door, and he could not relax. His relationships with his adult children grew strained; he refused to join them for dinner at crowded restaurants, claiming fatigue. What frightened him most was the loss of control—the sense that his own body’s reactions were dictating his life. He had come to believe that if he did not stay vigilant, the dizziness would incapacitate him, and he would be trapped, helpless, just as he had been on that riverbank.

Finally, after a particularly bad episode where he had to leave his classroom mid-lesson, his principal gently suggested he take a leave of absence. That afternoon, Carlos called a therapist who specialized in trauma. He was not sure he could talk about the ambush, but he knew he could not keep running from the taste, the dizziness, and the sounds that followed him everywhere. He hoped that someone could help him stop checking for exits long enough to breathe.
